questions.stimulus:
I. The uproar over a former army chief’s unpublished memoir is less about one book and more
about how a democracy negotiates the uneasy space between national security, political
accountability, and historical truth. When fragments of a still-uncleared manuscript begin
shaping parliamentary debate, the real story is not just what is written on those pages, but why
those pages have become so sensitive in the first place.


At the heart of the controversy lies the memory of a crisis that still unsettles the public
imagination: a high-altitude confrontation that cost lives and altered the strategic climate along
a contested border. Decisions taken ~ or deferred ~ during those weeks inevitably become part
of the nation’s strategic folklore. It is precisely this grey zone, where military judgment meets
political direction, that memoirs seek to illuminate and governments often prefer to keep
shaded. There is a legitimate argument for caution. Operational details, command procedures,
and sensitive assessments cannot be treated like material for casual disclosure. No serious state
can allow its security architecture to be reverse-engineered through personal recollections.
Clearance processes exist for a reason, and retired officers are not private citizens in quite the
same way as retired teachers or diplomats. The uniform, even when folded away, leaves behind
obligations. Yet, prolonged silence and opaque delays create their own problems.


When a manuscript lingers in limbo, it invites speculation, leaks, and selective quotation.
Snippets then acquire a political life of their own, detached from context, sharpened into
weapons for daily combat in Parliament. What should have been a sober debate about process
and precedent becomes another shouting match, with rules and patriotism hurled at each other
like slogans. This is not healthy for civil-military relations or for democratic oversight. A
republic does not honour its armed forces by turning every uncomfortable question into an act
of disloyalty. Nor does it strengthen national security by pretending that strategic episodes can
be sealed off from historical scrutiny forever. The public does not need theatrics; it needs clarity
about how decisions are made when the stakes involve lives, territory, and long-term
deterrence.

II. Philip arrived on the first day of the new year, eager, he announced, to get to work. He was
plump and pale, and reeked of mildew or worse, and he arrived with a dog about whom he had
informed no one. Still, pets were not expressly forbidden. The dog had a melancholy air.
“What’s its name?” I asked.
“What!” Philip demanded.
I helped him unpack his vehicle. There was no luggage, but there were a great many tightly
sealed cardboard boxes.
“Would you like me to get additional supplies?” I asked. “Dog food?”
“What?” Philip bellowed again. “I’m anxious to get down to business.”
I said that the guests, the Fellows, always remarked on how astonishingly quickly their time
here went by.
“What! That’s preposterous! Time never goes anywhere!”
The dog followed me outside and sniffed the tires of my truck. Together, we studied the sky,
which appeared threatening. I rearranged some porch furniture. The dog looked at me. If I were
to attempt to describe that look I would say that it was one that deeply questioned what it was
looking at, my very existence even. We walked toward the woods and I showed him various


breaks in the fence line. “Don’t go out there,” I advised him, “unless you’re accompanied by
someone, preferably a person.”
“You mean like Philip,” he said, though of course he couldn’t have. We went back into the
house and he settled onto a bed that had been prepared for him, a nest of faded beach towels.
He chewed thoughtfully at a hole in one of them.


I told Philip about the weather-alert system, the emergency phone, the extra batteries and
candles, the German vacuum cleaner which no Fellow had ever mastered. Once again, I asked
him the dog’s name but he didn’t seem to hear me. He said he was working on a major work,
an exceedingly major work.
“No one will bother you,” I assured him. “The university doesn’t care about this place. I think
they’d just as soon tear it down.”
“Why not,” he agreed. He seemed more cheerful now that I was leaving. That evening, it began
to rain. When it stopped raining, I ventured out to visit the residency, but the creek was
impassable.

III. New research suggests that AI’s “thought” processes may be more similar to those of
humans than previously suspected. Here’s how: You’re scrolling endlessly through all the junk
on X. The memes, the insults, the fake news and conspiracy theories, the gender wars and literal
wars. Pause, and take a deep breath — it’s starting to get to you, isn’t it? Consuming junk data
isn’t productive; it’s destructive. It won’t enhance your understanding; it’ll give you brain rot.


And here’s the clincher: It’ll affect an LLM in exactly the same way. Take a bow, AI — you’re
getting closer to humanity.


A preprint study by researchers from Texas A&M University, the University of Texas at Austin
and Purdue University has found that AI can indeed get brain rot. Exposing LLMs to junk data
from X led to declines in “reasoning, long-context understanding, safety, and inflating ‘dark
traits’ (e.g., psychopathy, narcissism)”. And once an AI goes down that route, there’s no
coming back — attempts to “heal” the LLMs using clean data were only partially successful.


Fears of AI turning “dark” aren’t just sci-fi hypotheticals; they reflect today’s fast-changing
realities. There are more and more reports about conversations with AI leading to suicide — in
one case, a chatbot discouraged a teen in the US from seeking help, and offered to write a
suicide note — as well as crimes including murder. Another danger is the erosion of humans’
ability to carry out research for themselves or compose a simple piece of writing. It won’t be
hard for psychopathic robots to one day conquer a species that has outsourced thought. Perhaps
the brain rot itself is the best defence — the would-be AI overlords may be too busy memeing
to murder. The best part? This editorial was written by a human being.

IV. All too often, in this age of disconnection and scattered focus, employee dissatisfaction is
expressed in symbolic gestures — individual acts of defiance that amount to “lying down” on
the job (tang ping as practised by China’s youth, for example) or doing the bare minimum (as
seen in the post-pandemic wave of “quiet quitting”). Creating ripples that quietly and quickly


dissipate, there is little about these actions that inspires change or provokes a reaction. Before
the great, well-oiled machinery of capital and industry, they are the most minor of irritants,
abstractions that are easy to brush aside or roll over.


Which is what makes the protest launched last Saturday by workers at a toll plaza on the Agra-
Lucknow highway remarkable. Unhappy over the paltry Diwali bonus they received, 21
staffers raised the barriers and walked off the job, thus allowing over 5,000 vehicles to breeze
through without paying the hefty toll: An elegant execution of the hit-em-where-it-hurts school
of attack usually reserved for the boxing or wrestling ring. As an act of protest against an
employer trying to economise at the expense of workers, it doesn’t get more impactful than
this. Not surprisingly, the company operating the toll booth agreed that very night to hike the
striking staffers’ pay.


Beyond being a Diwali miracle of sorts, the episode is an affirmation of why the underdog story
continues to matter. It’s easy enough to throw up one’s hands, allow the big and small
indignities of the everyday to erode the will to fight and replace what could be a rallying cry
with a sigh of defeat. The protest in that one toll plaza in Uttar Pradesh comes, then, as a
reminder that the small guy, too, can win — all it takes is collective will and knowing where
to hit.

V. Rome wasn’t built in a day, but 22-year-old Alcaraz beating 38-year-old Djokovic at
Australian Open is yet another reminder that coming of age needn’t take forever. Nasa took
just 11 years to touch down on Moon. Japan was running rings around US car industry, in
America, after 20 years. India went from being milkdeficient to the largest producer 28 years
after launch of Op Flood. Yet, almost 80 years after Independence, our millennia-old agriculture
and dairy are considered incapable of standing up to foreign competition, therefore, in need of
tariff protection.


This is clear from trade agreements signed over the past 12 months. Whether it is CETA with
UK, or the FTA with New Zealand, and now the EU and US deals, agriculture and dairy always
become sticking points for India. It’s no secret that ink on the deal with Trump would have
dried early last year, but for India’s political compulsions based on its vast farmer population.
Now, no country is immune to such pressures. France, even though it has fewer than 4L farming
households, as against up to 15cr in India, has seen strong resistance to EU’s recent trade deal
with S America’s Mercosur block. And that’s understandable because food security is part of
national security. Jawan and kisan together win wars.


But India’s resistance to agri imports – commerce minister has said “India is never going to
open up dairy” – is not about Jai Kisan . Rather, it’s an acknowledgement of the precarity of
our farmers. Farming accounts for only 1.2% of US employment. It makes up 1% of US GDP,
and 1.6% in EU. But it’s worth 16.3% of India’s far smaller GDP. Simply too many Indians are
eking out a living on small, unviable farms. Why? For want of better and dependable
employment. And because agriculture as a sector is growing far slower than the Indian
economy – 4.4% vs 7.4% – their prospects aren’t exactly bright.


So, India’s protectionist stand is justified, but for how long? That’s the Rome question. How
many more decades will it take us to reduce agricultural population to, say, 20%, or 10%?
Because keeping 45% of population in an unproductive sector is like parking money in a low-
interest savings account. It’s a waste of India’s demographic dividend. India should show
greater urgency to absorb farmers in the industrial workforce. So that 10 or 15 years from now,
every FTA does not seem like a threat to half the population’s livelihood.

V. Rome wasn’t built in a day, but 22-year-old Alcaraz beating 38-year-old Djokovic at
Australian Open is yet another reminder that coming of age needn’t take forever. Nasa took
just 11 years to touch down on Moon. Japan was running rings around US car industry, in
America, after 20 years. India went from being milkdeficient to the largest producer 28 years
after launch of Op Flood. Yet, almost 80 years after Independence, our millennia-old agriculture
and dairy are considered incapable of standing up to foreign competition, therefore, in need of
tariff protection.


This is clear from trade agreements signed over the past 12 months. Whether it is CETA with
UK, or the FTA with New Zealand, and now the EU and US deals, agriculture and dairy always
become sticking points for India. It’s no secret that ink on the deal with Trump would have
dried early last year, but for India’s political compulsions based on its vast farmer population.
Now, no country is immune to such pressures. France, even though it has fewer than 4L farming
households, as against up to 15cr in India, has seen strong resistance to EU’s recent trade deal
with S America’s Mercosur block. And that’s understandable because food security is part of
national security. Jawan and kisan together win wars.


But India’s resistance to agri imports – commerce minister has said “India is never going to
open up dairy” – is not about Jai Kisan . Rather, it’s an acknowledgement of the precarity of
our farmers. Farming accounts for only 1.2% of US employment. It makes up 1% of US GDP,
and 1.6% in EU. But it’s worth 16.3% of India’s far smaller GDP. Simply too many Indians are
eking out a living on small, unviable farms. Why? For want of better and dependable
employment. And because agriculture as a sector is growing far slower than the Indian
economy – 4.4% vs 7.4% – their prospects aren’t exactly bright.


So, India’s protectionist stand is justified, but for how long? That’s the Rome question. How
many more decades will it take us to reduce agricultural population to, say, 20%, or 10%?
Because keeping 45% of population in an unproductive sector is like parking money in a low-
interest savings account. It’s a waste of India’s demographic dividend. India should show
greater urgency to absorb farmers in the industrial workforce. So that 10 or 15 years from now,
every FTA does not seem like a threat to half the population’s livelihood.

LEGAL REASONING

IX. The incorporation of prerogative writs into the Indian Constitution represents a
sophisticated legal transplant, adapting English common law remedies to serve a
transformative constitutional purpose. While originating as royal commands from the King's
Bench in England to control inferior tribunals and officials, these writs were strategically
enshrined in Articles 32 and 226 to become the primary engines for enforcing the new social
contract between the state and the citizen. Their evolution from tools of monarchical oversight
to bulwarks of a republican democracy underscores a deliberate constitutional design. The
Supreme Court and High Courts, designated as "guardians of the Constitution," wield these
writs not merely as judicial remedies but as instruments for maintaining constitutional
equilibrium. This function extends beyond individual grievance redressal to encompass a
broader structural role: ensuring that all organs of the state remain within the boundaries of
power demarcated by the Constitution.


This structural mandate is particularly evident in the expansion of the writ jurisdiction's scope.
While the named writs—Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo
Warranto—provide a categorized framework, Indian judiciary has transcended their rigid
historical definitions. The creative interpretation of "for any other purpose" in Article 226 has
empowered High Courts to fashion innovative orders and directions, effectively crafting a
unique jurisprudence of constitutional remedies. This flexibility allows the judiciary to address
the complexities of a modern administrative state, where abuse of power can take forms
unanticipated by traditional writ categories. Consequently, the writ system performs a dual
function: it is both a shield for the citizen's rights and a sentinel over constitutional morality,
continuously defining the limits of permissible state action. The ongoing judicial articulation
of writ principles thus constitutes a dynamic dialogue on the nature of state power and
individual liberty within India's constitutional scheme, making it a cornerstone of the world's
largest democracy.

X. The Indian Penal Code meticulously structures offences against the state, creating a
hierarchy of gravity. Sections 124, 124A, 125, and 126 collectively demonstrate the law’s aim
to protect both internal constitutional order and external diplomatic peace, though they operate
in starkly different legal climates.

Section 124 serves a precise, protective function for India’s constitutional framework. It
criminalises assault or illegal restraint of the President or a Governor, but crucially, only when
accompanied by the specific intent to compel or restrain the exercise of any lawful power. This


mens rea transforms a serious crime against a person into a profound offence against the state
itself, as it seeks to manipulate sovereign authority through force. Punishable by imprisonment
for life or up to seven years and a fine, its severity underscores the inviolability of the
constitutional offices, ensuring that the exercise of lawful power remains free from coercive
violence.

In stark contrast lies the infamous Section 124A—sedition—a provision currently in a state of
constitutional suspension. Historically defined as bringing hatred, contempt, or disaffection
towards the government, its broad phrasing led to severe criticism for stifling legitimate
dissent. In a landmark 2022 ruling, the Supreme Court effectively suspended its operation,
staying all pending cases and barring new registrations until a governmental review. The Court
contemporaneously narrowed its possible future scope, clarifying that only incitement to
imminent violence or public disorder could potentially be culpable, thereby insulating strong
criticism from its ambit. This judicial intervention has placed this colonial-era provision, which
still carries a potential life sentence on paper, in profound abeyance.

Moving from internal authority to international comity, Sections 125 and 126 externalise this
protective principle. Section 125 criminalises waging war against any Asiatic power allied with
India, imposing life imprisonment. This reflects India’s commitment to regional stability and
treaty obligations. Complementing this, Section 126 addresses “depredation”—essentially
state-on-state plunder or robbery—on territories of any power at peace with India. Punishable
with up to seven years’ imprisonment, fine, and forfeiture of property, it functions as a statutory
deterrent against private actors committing acts of aggression that could jeopardise
international relations.

Thus, while Section 124 guards the pinnacle of domestic constitutional machinery, and the
contested 124A touches upon expressions against the government, Sections 125 and 126
project the state’s protective mandate outward, safeguarding friendly nations from hostile acts
originating within Indian territory. Together, they form a legal bulwark designed to secure the
republic’s sovereignty and its peaceful standing in the world.

questions.stimulus:
X. The Indian Penal Code meticulously structures offences against the state, creating a
hierarchy of gravity. Sections 124, 124A, 125, and 126 collectively demonstrate the law’s aim
to protect both internal constitutional order and external diplomatic peace, though they operate
in starkly different legal climates.

Section 124 serves a precise, protective function for India’s constitutional framework. It
criminalises assault or illegal restraint of the President or a Governor, but crucially, only when
accompanied by the specific intent to compel or restrain the exercise of any lawful power. This


mens rea transforms a serious crime against a person into a profound offence against the state
itself, as it seeks to manipulate sovereign authority through force. Punishable by imprisonment
for life or up to seven years and a fine, its severity underscores the inviolability of the
constitutional offices, ensuring that the exercise of lawful power remains free from coercive
violence.

In stark contrast lies the infamous Section 124A—sedition—a provision currently in a state of
constitutional suspension. Historically defined as bringing hatred, contempt, or disaffection
towards the government, its broad phrasing led to severe criticism for stifling legitimate
dissent. In a landmark 2022 ruling, the Supreme Court effectively suspended its operation,
staying all pending cases and barring new registrations until a governmental review. The Court
contemporaneously narrowed its possible future scope, clarifying that only incitement to
imminent violence or public disorder could potentially be culpable, thereby insulating strong
criticism from its ambit. This judicial intervention has placed this colonial-era provision, which
still carries a potential life sentence on paper, in profound abeyance.

Moving from internal authority to international comity, Sections 125 and 126 externalise this
protective principle. Section 125 criminalises waging war against any Asiatic power allied with
India, imposing life imprisonment. This reflects India’s commitment to regional stability and
treaty obligations. Complementing this, Section 126 addresses “depredation”—essentially
state-on-state plunder or robbery—on territories of any power at peace with India. Punishable
with up to seven years’ imprisonment, fine, and forfeiture of property, it functions as a statutory
deterrent against private actors committing acts of aggression that could jeopardise
international relations.

Thus, while Section 124 guards the pinnacle of domestic constitutional machinery, and the
contested 124A touches upon expressions against the government, Sections 125 and 126
project the state’s protective mandate outward, safeguarding friendly nations from hostile acts
originating within Indian territory. Together, they form a legal bulwark designed to secure the
republic’s sovereignty and its peaceful standing in the world.

questions.stimulus:
XI. The solemnization and dissolution of Christian marriages in India are primarily governed
by two colonial-era statutes: the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872 (ICMA) and the Indian
Divorce Act, 1869 (IDA), the latter substantially amended in 2001. The ICMA meticulously
regulates the solemnization process. A Christian marriage may be solemnized by an ordained
Minister of Religion, within the limits of their church, or by a Marriage Registrar appointed
under the Act. The procedure typically involves the issuance of public notice, a waiting period
for objections, and the mandatory presence of at least two witnesses during the ceremony.
Subsequently, the marriage must be registered in a marriage register, and a certificate is issued,
serving as crucial evidence of the union.

For a marriage to be valid under this framework, it must fulfill several conditions. It is strictly
monogamous, prohibiting any party from having a living spouse. The parties must have
attained the legal age of marriage—21 years for the groom and 18 years for the bride. Both
must be of sound mind at the time of marriage, capable of providing free, informed consent.
Crucially, consent must not be obtained by force, fraud, or undue influence. Furthermore, the
law prohibits marriages within certain degrees of consanguinity (blood relations) and affinity


(relations by marriage), preventing unions between close kin such as siblings, or an uncle and
niece.

The IDA distinguishes between void and voidable marriages. A marriage is void ab initio (from
the beginning) if it contravenes the essential conditions, such as being bigamous, falling within
the prohibited degrees of relationship, or involving a party incapable of consent due to
unsoundness of mind. These marriages are considered legally non-existent. Conversely, a
voidable marriage is valid until annulled by a court decree. Grounds for annulment include the
respondent’s impotence preventing consummation, either party’s incurable unsoundness of
mind, the respondent’s willful refusal to consummate, the wife’s pregnancy by another at the
time of marriage (unknown to the husband), or consent being obtained by fraud or force. A
petition for annulment on these grounds must be filed within specific statutory time limits from
the discovery of the cause.

questions.stimulus:
XII. The Indian Constitution vests the judiciary with the profound responsibility of acting as
the guardian of fundamental rights and the ultimate arbiter of constitutional validity. Beyond
the specific doctrines applied in adjudication, this role necessitates a foundational framework
for evaluating state action. A core aspect of this framework is the interpretation of Article 14,
which guarantees the right to equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. The
Supreme Court has consistently held that Article 14 is not a sterile abstraction but a dynamic
guarantee that strikes at arbitrariness in state action. This has led to the development of a
nuanced two-pronged test for assessing the validity of any legislative or administrative
classification.

The first and traditional principle is that of "reasonable classification." The state is permitted
to classify persons or objects for the purpose of legislation, but such classification must be
founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes those grouped together from others
left out. Crucially, this differentia must have a rational nexus to the legitimate object sought to
be achieved by the law. This test allows the government to enact laws for specific sections of
society or to address particular problems, provided the basis for distinction is logical and just.
For instance, a law imposing higher taxes on luxury goods creates a classification based on the
nature of the commodity, with a direct nexus to the object of generating revenue based on
capacity to pay.

The second, more potent, expansion is the "arbitrariness" doctrine. Propounded decisively in
the case of E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu and later solidified in Maneka Gandhi v.
Union of India, this principle holds that equality is a antithesis of arbitrariness. Consequently,
any state action—whether legislative or executive—that is arbitrary, capricious, or without
adequate determining principle, violates Article 14. This doctrine infuses the concept of
fairness and non-arbitrariness into every state action, acting as a powerful check against mere
whim or abuse of power. It demands that decisions, even those adhering to a formal procedure,
must be based on relevant and rational considerations. This interpretive stride has allowed the
judiciary to scrutinize the substance and fairness of state action, ensuring that the guarantee of


equality is not merely procedural but profoundly substantive. Through this evolving
interpretation, Article 14 has become a comprehensive shield against unfair and unreasonable
treatment by the state, embodying the essence of justice and fairness in a democratic polity.

questions.stimulus:
XIII. The tort of private nuisance serves as a crucial legal mechanism for resolving conflicts
between neighboring landowners, providing a remedy for an unreasonable, substantial, and
unlawful interference with one’s use or enjoyment of their property. The interference, which
forms the basis of the claim, can manifest in tangible forms such as flooding, vibrations, or
invasive roots, or in intangible forms like persistent noise, light pollution, or noxious odors.
This interference may stem from an ongoing activity on the defendant’s land or from a static
physical condition, such as a dangerously decayed tree threatening to fall.

Central to the claim is the requirement that the interference be “unreasonable.” This is an
objective standard, measured not by the plaintiff’s personal sensitivity but by its effect on a
person of ordinary sensibilities. Courts employ a balancing test, weighing the gravity of the
harm inflicted upon the plaintiff against the social utility of the defendant’s conduct. In this
calculus, key factors include the extent, duration, and character of the interference, the
suitability of the activity to its locality, and whether the defendant employed all reasonable
precautions. Consequently, operating a factory in an industrial district may be deemed
reasonable, whereas generating identical noise and smoke in a residential neighborhood likely
is not.

The harm suffered must also be “substantial,” meaning it materially and significantly affects
the property’s comfort, health, or usability, beyond a mere trifling annoyance. Furthermore,
standing is strictly limited to individuals possessing a property interest in the affected land,
such as owners or tenants; a mere guest or visitor lacks the legal right to sue. Successful
plaintiffs may seek two primary remedies. Compensatory damages are awarded for past and
ongoing harms, including property value reduction, lost rental income, and personal
discomfort. Alternatively, or in addition, a court may issue an injunction—a discretionary order
commanding the defendant to abate the nuisance. Courts hesitate to grant injunctions where
the hardship to the defendant and community would be grossly disproportionate to the
plaintiff’s benefit, sometimes awarding “damages in lieu of an injunction.” In narrowly defined
situations, a plaintiff may engage in reasonable self-help, such as cutting intruding branches,
though this approach carries legal risk if exercised improperly.

XIV. The constitutional architecture of Indian federalism ingeniously embeds a mechanism for
the periodic recalibration of fiscal power between the Union and the States: the Finance
Commission. Established under Article 280, this quasi-judicial body serves as the linchpin of
vertical and horizontal devolution, tasked with ensuring a structured and principled distribution
of national resources. Its primary mandate is to recommend the division of the net proceeds of
taxes between the Centre and the States and the allocation of the States’ share among
themselves. This process, repeated every five years, is not merely an accounting exercise but a
profound exercise in balancing the principles of equity, efficiency, and need within a vast and
diverse federation.

The Commission’s work is fundamentally guided by the constitutional directive to foster
"equitable sharing" based on an objective assessment of states' fiscal capacities and needs. This
involves complex considerations, weighing factors like income distance, geographical area,
and population to address horizontal imbalances. A state with lower per capita income, for
instance, may receive a higher share to equalize its capacity to provide public services.
Simultaneously, the Commission must ensure the Union government retains sufficient fiscal
space to discharge its responsibilities for national defense, foreign affairs, and macroeconomic
stability—a constant tension at the heart of its deliberations. The recommendations extend


beyond tax devolution to encompass grants-in-aid, providing crucial support to states with
revenue deficits or specific needs that the formula cannot fully address.

The evolution of the Finance Commission’s role mirrors India’s changing economic and
political landscape. Initially focused on bridging budgetary gaps, its terms of reference have
expanded to incorporate contemporary challenges like promoting fiscal discipline, funding
local governance institutions, and addressing new priorities like disaster management. Each
Commission thus interprets its constitutional mandate through a contemporary lens, navigating
the competing demands of assertive states and a Union government with pan-national
responsibilities. Its success lies in its non-political, expert-driven approach, which lends
legitimacy to its often-contested recommendations. Ultimately, the Finance Commission is
more than a fiscal arbitrator; it is a vital institution of cooperative federalism, striving to
translate constitutional principles of unity and shared prosperity into a working financial
formula that holds a vast and unequal union together.

XIV. The constitutional architecture of Indian federalism ingeniously embeds a mechanism for
the periodic recalibration of fiscal power between the Union and the States: the Finance
Commission. Established under Article 280, this quasi-judicial body serves as the linchpin of
vertical and horizontal devolution, tasked with ensuring a structured and principled distribution
of national resources. Its primary mandate is to recommend the division of the net proceeds of
taxes between the Centre and the States and the allocation of the States’ share among
themselves. This process, repeated every five years, is not merely an accounting exercise but a
profound exercise in balancing the principles of equity, efficiency, and need within a vast and
diverse federation.

The Commission’s work is fundamentally guided by the constitutional directive to foster
"equitable sharing" based on an objective assessment of states' fiscal capacities and needs. This
involves complex considerations, weighing factors like income distance, geographical area,
and population to address horizontal imbalances. A state with lower per capita income, for
instance, may receive a higher share to equalize its capacity to provide public services.
Simultaneously, the Commission must ensure the Union government retains sufficient fiscal
space to discharge its responsibilities for national defense, foreign affairs, and macroeconomic
stability—a constant tension at the heart of its deliberations. The recommendations extend


beyond tax devolution to encompass grants-in-aid, providing crucial support to states with
revenue deficits or specific needs that the formula cannot fully address.

The evolution of the Finance Commission’s role mirrors India’s changing economic and
political landscape. Initially focused on bridging budgetary gaps, its terms of reference have
expanded to incorporate contemporary challenges like promoting fiscal discipline, funding
local governance institutions, and addressing new priorities like disaster management. Each
Commission thus interprets its constitutional mandate through a contemporary lens, navigating
the competing demands of assertive states and a Union government with pan-national
responsibilities. Its success lies in its non-political, expert-driven approach, which lends
legitimacy to its often-contested recommendations. Ultimately, the Finance Commission is
more than a fiscal arbitrator; it is a vital institution of cooperative federalism, striving to
translate constitutional principles of unity and shared prosperity into a working financial
formula that holds a vast and unequal union together.

questions.stimulus:
XVIII. At a United Nations meeting about climate change, 16-year-old Greta Thunberg gave a
passionate and angry speech. She criticized people who haven't done enough to stop global
warming. Some people didn't like her speech because they thought her anger would push away
people who might otherwise support the cause. While anger can sometimes make people feel
left out or uncomfortable, many feel Thunberg's anger makes sense. After all, years of pollution
and industrial growth got us into this crisis.
Thunberg's speech highlights a long-standing debate. On one side are people who think anger
is harmful because it doesn't help solve problems. On the other side are those who believe anger
is a natural and useful emotion, both in public life and personal situations. We see this question
come up again and again—from the righteous, worldwide anger that launched the 2017
Women’s March, the day after Donald Trump’s inauguration as president of the United States,
to the violent protests in Hong Kong, to the fearful demonstrations against a new citizenship
law in India. The basic question is always: Is anger useful?
The ancient philosopher Aristotle described anger as a painful feeling that makes us want
revenge when we or someone close to us is treated unfairly. Anger is a reaction to something
that feels wrong, and it includes a desire for payback. Think about when someone you trusted
lied to you, or when your favorite bike was stolen. It hurt, but it also made you feel like you
deserved an explanation.


Modern philosopher Amia Srinivasan argues that anger has real value. She explains that anger
can help people understand their own suffering better. When victims of injustice feel angry,
their emotions become sharper and help them focus on exactly what was done to them. This
anger can actually help them make sense of their situation and understand their oppression
more clearly.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “The fruits of anger”, aeon.]

XIX. India spends only 0.6% of its GDP on research and development—far less than China's
2.4% and Brazil's 1.3%. Even more troubling, private companies contribute just one-third of
this amount. If India wants to become a global economic leader, this must change dramatically.


The government has shown commitment through initiatives like the ₹1 lakh crore Research,
Development and Innovation Scheme announced in the 2025-26 Budget. This includes funding
for deep-tech investments, support for the National Quantum Mission, and continued backing
for semiconductor manufacturing. These steps aim to strengthen India's research ecosystem.
Yet private companies remain reluctant to invest their own money in R&D. This hesitation
makes sense. The domestic market rarely rewards innovative products with higher prices, and
government procurement doesn't reliably purchase homegrown innovations. A recent RBI
study confirms that corporate investment optimism actually fell in 2024-25.
Look at how innovation happens globally. Private risk capital, combined with public support,
drives major breakthroughs—with companies leading large-scale applied research.
Consider Meta, which operates roughly 600,000 GPUs costing billions. Google plans to double
its computing capacity every six months to meet AI demand. Their deal with Anthropic,
reportedly worth tens of billions, aims to add over a million GPUs by 2026. No government
could match such investment without exhausting its entire R&D budget.
We saw a similar pattern with data centres. Despite government subsidies, significant private
investment only followed after enterprise demand proved the market existed.
For India to transform its R&D landscape, the private sector needs more than government
schemes. It needs confidence that bold risks will be rewarded. Companies must believe that
investing in differentiated technology makes business sense—that innovative products will
find buyers and early adopters.
Creating this enabling environment means aligning market incentives with innovation. When
private firms see that R&D investment directly connects to growth and profits, they will move
from the margins to the mainstream. Only then can India match its industrial ambitions with
world-class research and development.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “India’s tech ambitions need private sector investment
in R&D. Budget 2026 holds the key”, ThePrint.]
